label: BASIC + visual forms
citation: Cooper, A. (1996). Why I am called "the Father of Visual Basic". cooper.com (essay; read via hn-classics mirror).
quote: Microsoft took advantage of this dynamic interface to unplug our little shell language and replace it entirely with QuickBasic.
note: Original URL http://www.cooper.com/alan/father_of_vb.html is now 404; Cooper also writes the interface 'would be completely manipulable by drag and drop'. The BASIC lineage runs via Microsoft QuickBasic, not Dartmouth BASIC directly; CHM's 2017 Fellow profile corroborates (Ruby paired with QBasic, released 1990).

label: VB inside Office
citation: Microsoft (n.d.). Visual Basic for Applications Frequently Asked Questions. MSDN (Previous Versions).
quote: VBA offers the same powerful tools as Visual Basic in the context of an existing application
note: The VB6 docs (learn.microsoft.com/.../visual-basic-6/aa240839) add that VBA (Vba6.dll) 'is the underlying language engine for Visual Basic' and 'is included in Microsoft Office', so the two share one language core.

label: "Borland's answer" (product competition)
citation: Thorpe, D. (n.d.). Why the name "Delphi?". Borland Museum, Embarcadero.
quote: making Delphi a database product was exactly what was needed to break Borland's Pascal tools out of the Visual Basic – C++ market squeeze play
note: Thorpe was on the original Delphi team. Marco Cantù (marcocantu.com/delphibirth) reports another name that circulated was 'VBK (Visual Basic Killer)'. This documents market competition, not a language-design influence.

label: turtle, learning by tinkering (Resnick)
citation: Resnick, M. (2022). 10 sparks that lit the flame of Scratch. Medium.
quote: The Logo programming language was, in many ways, the most important inspiration for Scratch.
note: The same post describes Logo's turtle. In Resnick et al. (2009, CACM, 'Scratch: Programming for All') the 'tinkering' design ideal is credited to LEGO bricks, and Papert's 'low floor / high ceiling' to Logo.
suggested_label: Papert's Logo: turtle programming, low floor

label: procedural extensions
citation: Microsoft (n.d.). Describe T-SQL for programming. Microsoft Learn training module 'Get started with Transact-SQL programming'.
quote: While SQL is a programming language, T-SQL adds support for procedural programming and the use of local variables.
note: The page also says T-SQL 'is a proprietary extension of the open standard Structured Query Language (SQL)'.

label: procedural extensions
citation: Oracle (2019). Overview of PL/SQL. Oracle Database PL/SQL Language Reference, 19c.
quote: PL/SQL, the Oracle procedural extension of SQL, is a portable, high-performance transaction-processing language.
note: The page also says it 'combines the data-manipulating power of SQL with the processing power of procedural languages.'

label: SELECT syntax for cubes
citation: Microsoft (n.d.). MDX Query - The Basic Query. Analysis Services documentation, Microsoft Learn.
quote: The syntax format for the MDX SELECT statement is similar to that of SQL syntax.
note: This documents a deliberate syntactic resemblance rather than an explicit statement of design intent; the page goes on to list how the axes, FROM (one cube only) and WHERE (slicer) behave differently.

label: declarative keywords (Cypher's SQL-inspired keywords)
citation: Neo4j (n.d.). Cypher overview. Neo4j Cypher Manual.
quote: It was created in 2011 by Neo4j engineers as an SQL-equivalent language for graph databases.
note: The page also says Cypher and SQL 'share many of the same keywords, such as WHERE and ORDER BY'.

label: table & filter thinking
citation: Schreiber, L. (2018). Das Team hinter Power BI: Jeffrey Wang (interview, English version). SSBI-Blog.
quote: We had considered three existing programming languages: Excel formulas, SQL, MDX.
note: Wang (DAX engine lead) says SQL 'lacks the core BI concept of measure' and that DAX was built on 'simple relational database concepts like tables, columns, and relationships' with Excel-style syntax. Nothing ties filter context to SQL, and Microsoft's own docs call DAX an extension of the Excel formula language.
suggested_label: SQL weighed in design; relational table concepts

label: dplyr verbs via dplyr (library-mediated)
citation: Wickham, H., Çetinkaya-Rundel, M., & Grolemund, G. (2023). R for Data Science (2nd ed.), ch. 'Databases'. O'Reilly.
quote: Notice how desc() is translated to DESC: this is one of the many dplyr functions whose name was directly inspired by SQL.
note: A footnote on group_by() adds 'the dplyr function name was inspired by the SQL clause'. The influence is on the dplyr package, not on base R, which matches the 'library-mediated' label.

label: functional, F#-like
citation: Microsoft (n.d.). Power Query M formula language. Microsoft Learn.
quote: The M language is a functional, case-sensitive language similar to F#.
note: Microsoft states a similarity, not an influence. The M spec introduction (m-spec-introduction) calls M 'mostly pure, higher-order, dynamically typed, partially lazy', models its evaluation on spreadsheets, and does not mention F#.
suggested_label: functional; Microsoft calls it 'similar to F#'

label: Cocoa object model, named arguments, ARC
quote: Swift also borrows from other languages, for instance named parameters brought forward from Objective-C are expressed in a clean syntax that makes APIs in Swift easy to read and maintain.
note: For ARC, The Swift Programming Language's ARC chapter says 'Using ARC in Swift is very similar to the approach described in Transitioning to ARC Release Notes for using ARC with Objective-C.' 'Cocoa object model' was not found verbatim; swift.org only says Apple platforms include the Objective-C runtime to reach UIKit and AppKit.
suggested_label: named parameters, ARC, Obj-C runtime interop

label: safety and ownership ideas
citation: Lattner, C. (2016, July 29). Looking back on Swift 3 and ahead to Swift 4. swift-evolution (Swift Forums).
quote: Adding an (opt-in) Cyclone/Rust inspired memory ownership model to Swift is highly desired by systems programmers
note: The Swift Ownership Manifesto (swift/docs/OwnershipManifesto.md) notes 'many similarities between shared values and Rust's concept of an immutable borrow'. Lattner's homepage lists Rust among Swift's sources of ideas. The ownership part is well supported; a general 'safety' influence is not specifically documented.

label: readability ideas
citation: Lattner, C., interviewed by Arment, M., Liss, C., & Siracusa, J. (2017). ATP Episode 205: Chris Lattner Interview Transcript. Accidental Tech Podcast.
quote: just like in Python, you can start with just print("Hello world"). You can do the exact same thing in Swift
note: Lattner's homepage (nondot.org/sabre) lists Python among the languages Swift drew ideas from, but names no feature. The only concrete point found is approachability (script-like top-level code / progressive disclosure); 'readability' is not specified.

label: protocols ~ type classes, Optional ~ Maybe
citation: Lattner, C., interviewed by Arment, M., Liss, C., & Siracusa, J. (2017). ATP Episode 205: Chris Lattner Interview Transcript. Accidental Tech Podcast.
quote: If you're a Haskell nerd, there is tons of Haskell concepts built in. Protocols really are just like a very similar Haskell construct, for example.
note: Lattner does not name the construct; reading it as type classes is an inference. No Lattner or Apple source found that ties Optional to Maybe, and the Swift Generics Manifesto does not mention Haskell. Lattner's homepage lists Haskell among Swift's sources of ideas.
suggested_label: protocols akin to Haskell type classes
